walkthroughs.body_html:
The Physical Environment — a core area of A-Level Environmental Science.

Working through it builds the schema you need: the key terms, how they connect, and how to use them together.

The Physical Environment brings together several ideas you need to use as a set, not in isolation.

Lock in the vocabulary first, then practise pulling the ideas together to answer real questions.

Use the activities in this adventure to build familiarity with The Physical Environment.

Practise vocabulary, calculations and free-text questions to lock in the learning.

mcqs.q: Which cycle has no significant atmospheric phase?
options: Carbon
Nitrogen
Phosphorus
Sulfur

mcqs.q: Average time in a reservoir is called?
options: Flux
Residence time
Lifetime
Half-life

mcqs.q: What is transpiration in the water cycle?
options: The movement of water through soil into rivers.
Phosphorus does not cycle at all.
The freezing of water into ice in glaciers.
The loss of water vapour from plant leaves to the atmosphere.

mcqs.q: Why is most atmospheric nitrogen unavailable to plants directly?
options: The freezing of water into ice in glaciers.
Plants cannot absorb any gases at all.
Nitrogen gas (N2) is very unreactive and must be fixed into compounds before plants can use it.
There is too little nitrogen in the air for plants to use.

mcqs.q: Does the phosphorus cycle have a significant gaseous (atmospheric) phase?
options: Phosphorus does not cycle at all.
Yes; phosphorus moves largely as a gas like carbon and nitrogen.
Plants cannot absorb any gases at all.
No; phosphorus cycles mainly through rock, soil and water with no major gaseous stage.

mcqs.q: Which of these is the best definition of “Biogeochemical cycle”?
options: Slow, sedimentary cycle: weathering of rocks releases phosphate; runs through life and back to ocean sediments.
Human alteration of natural fluxes (e.g., Haber process doubled global reactive N input).
Pathway by which a chemical element moves through biotic and abiotic compartments of Earth.
Compartment storing a quantity of an element, e.g., ocean carbon, soil nitrogen.
